# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

   | a park | anything else — leave the issue open, wearing exactly one of the four below |

   A park is ONE label, and its kind says what you are asking
   a person for. Pick by the REMEDY, not by how the run felt:

   | sub-label | when |
   |---|---|
   | `task:status:needs-human-approval` | you succeeded and deliberately left an unmerged PR. Name it; the human merges or closes it |
   | `task:status:needs-human-action` | something outside the code must change before this can run: a secret, a scope, a routine's wiring, an input this item never carried |
   | `task:status:needs-human-decision` | you stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice — you ran out of time, or you exceeded the declared ceiling and someone must say whether that stands |
   | `task:status:needs-human-failure` | the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or forged item. Use this when you are unsure |

   **A convergence you could not perform at all is the failure park, and never
   anything else.** Not `decision` (that is for a choice you stopped in front
   of), not `action` (that is for something outside the code that must change
   first). This is not a judgment call: the failure park is the only one that
   HOLDS THE TASK'S LANE, and a run that could not converge must stop its task
   recurring until a person has looked. Choosing a lane-releasing park here is
   how one broken convergence became fourteen stranded items in a member repo,
   one a night, each looking like a fresh incident.

   **Pass `--pr` on any park a pull request or an issue would end**, not only on an
   approval, where it is required. It stamps `Ends-when: #<n> closed` on the item, and
   that is what makes the park end by itself: the janitor closes the item `done` when
   the target merges and `rejected` when it is closed unmerged. Without it the park
   stands until a person happens to read it. **Pass it on a `done` too when your run
   landed a pull request**: on an item carrying `Supersedes:`, the pull request you
   name is what the earlier ones were waiting to be replaced by, and the command
   plans their closes only when it is given one.

   **A marked issue needs no write-back at all**: it is the item, so the approval
   park it wears *is* the in-review state and the failure park *is* the report (which
   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.

- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.

- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.

Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.

Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.

- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

1	# Growth — dedup local packs against the canon (per repo)
2	
3	Reconcile this repo's **local packs** against the shared **canon** it consumes (Claudinite, vendored read-only), pruning local items — a pack's prose line, or a whole local check —
4	the canon now covers. It lands the run's prunes through a single PR against the repo's default branch.
5	Often there's nothing to prune, and that's fine. The run's
6	**Context** is **binding scope — not a hint**: do not re-decide or widen it.
7	
8	> This task only prunes local packs against the canon; lifting local items up into the canon is the central
9	> promote task's job (canon-side).
10	
11	## Conventions used in this doc
12	
13	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
14	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Updating the tracking issue and opening the PR go through the session's
15	  **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches
16	  only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or
17	  a cross-repo clone.
18	- **The mounted canon.** The exact canon revision this repo currently consumes — compare against *that*, not a
19	  live fetch. It is what `.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp (a promotion is visible here only
20	  once baselining has converged the mount to include it). Prune only against what the repo actually mounts.
21	- **The dispatch's Context narrows the *yardstick*, never the local surface.** When the Context names
22	  newly-changed canon packs ("Re-check local items against these newly-changed canon packs: …"), **those packs
23	  are this run's entire yardstick**: every prune must cite a line or rule id from one of *them*, and you never
24	  widen the comparison to the rest of the mounted canon. What is *not* narrowed is the local side — **every**
25	  local item is in play against those packs, whatever it is about. (Local pack names are unrelated to canon
26	  pack names, so there is nothing to match up.) A dispatch with **no** Context block carries no such bound: the
27	  precondition emits the list only when the mounted canon moved, and its other arm — the repo's own local packs
28	  changed — deliberately emits none, so that run compares the fresh local items against the whole mounted canon.
29	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) —
30	  everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. That's the corpus this task prunes within; the
31	  read-only mounted canon elsewhere under
32	  `.claudinite/` is never a prune target, only the yardstick you prune *against*.
33	
34	## Start by reading the canon window diff
35	
36	**Code-work already ran** — [worker.mjs](worker.mjs), the deterministic first phase of this task — and wrote
37	what the mounted canon **added** in this window into the tracking issue's body: per declared pack, the added
38	prose lines file by file, and the ids of any checks the window introduced. Your dispatch names that issue.
39	**Read it before opening a single local pack.**
40	
41	That brief is the run's *starting point*, not a second bound: the Context's pack list is still what a prune
42	may cite, so a local item covered by an older line in one of those packs is a legitimate prune when you can

# Growth — dedup local packs against the canon (per repo)

Reconcile this repo's **local packs** against the shared **canon** it consumes (Claudinite, vendored read-only), pruning local items — a pack's prose line, or a whole local check —
the canon now covers. It lands the run's prunes through a single PR against the repo's default branch.
Often there's nothing to prune, and that's fine. The run's
**Context** is **binding scope — not a hint**: do not re-decide or widen it.

> This task only prunes local packs against the canon; lifting local items up into the canon is the central
> promote task's job (canon-side).

## Conventions used in this doc

- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Updating the tracking issue and opening the PR go through the session's
  **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches
  only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or
  a cross-repo clone.
- **The mounted canon.** The exact canon revision this repo currently consumes — compare against *that*, not a
  live fetch. It is what `.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp (a promotion is visible here only
  once baselining has converged the mount to include it). Prune only against what the repo actually mounts.
- **The dispatch's Context narrows the *yardstick*, never the local surface.** When the Context names
  newly-changed canon packs ("Re-check local items against these newly-changed canon packs: …"), **those packs
  are this run's entire yardstick**: every prune must cite a line or rule id from one of *them*, and you never
  widen the comparison to the rest of the mounted canon. What is *not* narrowed is the local side — **every**
  local item is in play against those packs, whatever it is about. (Local pack names are unrelated to canon
  pack names, so there is nothing to match up.) A dispatch with **no** Context block carries no such bound: the
  precondition emits the list only when the mounted canon moved, and its other arm — the repo's own local packs
  changed — deliberately emits none, so that run compares the fresh local items against the whole mounted canon.
- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) —
  everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. That's the corpus this task prunes within; the
  read-only mounted canon elsewhere under
  `.claudinite/` is never a prune target, only the yardstick you prune *against*.

## Start by reading the canon window diff

**Code-work already ran** — [worker.mjs](worker.mjs), the deterministic first phase of this task — and wrote
what the mounted canon **added** in this window into the tracking issue's body: per declared pack, the added
prose lines file by file, and the ids of any checks the window introduced. Your dispatch names that issue.
**Read it before opening a single local pack.**

That brief is the run's *starting point*, not a second bound: the Context's pack list is still what a prune
may cite, so a local item covered by an older line in one of those packs is a legitimate prune when you can
quote that line. What the brief buys you is attention spent where the *new* coverage is, instead of re-reading
a corpus whose lines mostly predate this run. It is complete except where it says otherwise — a file whose
diff was too large to fetch, and a per-file line cap, are both stated in place with the remainder counted; go
read those files directly.

A window in which no declared canon pack moved says so, and that run compares the repo's fresh local items
against the mounted canon as a whole — the same as a dispatch with no Context block.

The [skill](../../skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md) owns what to do with the additions: which are candidates,
which prune nothing, and why a removed canon line is the reverse signal.

## The method lives in the skill

What to prune, strip, or rephrase; the keep-test (an item that says *more* than the canon stays; one that
only says it in repo-specific names goes); how a canon **check** covers an item more strongly than prose;
and the shrink-only discipline — all of that is owned by the
[**growth-dedup** skill](../../skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This
worker only frames the unattended run around it.

## Discipline

- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon line (or the
  covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson.
- **Open a single PR against `main`** from the branch your item names (`Target-branch:`) — one PR for the
  whole run's prunes, not one per item — never a direct push, and never a branch of your own. An earlier
  round's pull request still open closes as superseded once yours exists, which your converge performs when
  handed `--pr`. **Title the commit and the PR
  `Claudinite growth: dedup local packs`** — the `growth-write-scope` check keys on that title to certify the
  run pruned only the repo's local packs. Then **deliver it by the shared procedure —
  [deliver-pr.md](../../../../packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md)** — that procedure, never this file, owns
  whether and how the PR lands. What holds the prune bar is the quote-the-canon-line discipline above, the
  `dedup-prune-integrity` and `growth-write-scope` checks, and CI — never a reviewer's second look, which a
  wrongful prune is easy to wave through anyway. **Put the issue reference in the commit message** —
  `Refs #<n>` for this task's tracking issue (below), in the commit itself, not only the PR body. The repo's
  `basics` `task-lifecycle` check gates a PR on its commits referencing an issue, so a prune commit that cites
  none reds the repo's CI and blocks the merge.
- If an edit touches something a test reads, run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green before pushing.

## The brief, and the record

Code-work has already posted **this window's canon diff** as a comment on your own work item — the issue you
are reading. That comment is the brief this run starts from. **It is a required input**: a work item carrying
no such comment is a failed run, not a lighter one, so park it (`task:status:needs-human-action`) naming what is missing rather
than re-deriving the window yourself.

The prune's own commit and PR body are the record — there is no changelog file and no standing issue. Name
in the PR body what each prune removed and the canon line that now covers it, so the claim behind it is
reviewable where the diff is.

## Nothing downstream catches a wrong prune

Proving the mounted canon genuinely covers a local item before pruning it — and telling "the canon now owns
this" from "the canon states this too generally, keep the local cut" — is a **judgment call**. The PR carrying a prune can land with no reviewer downstream to catch
what the run got wrong: a real lesson pruned on a claim the canon does not actually make is gone.

## What this task must never do

- **Never edit the read-only canon** — it only prunes the repo's *local packs* against it, and the
  `growth-write-scope` check reds a run that touches anything outside them.
- **Never land a prune outside a PR** — every prune rides the run's single PR, delivered by
  [deliver-pr.md](../../../../packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md); a direct push to `main` is never in scope.
- **Never prune a local item without quoting the mounted-canon line (or covering check rule id) that covers
  it** — when unsure, leave it.
- **Never widen the dispatch's Context.** If it named the changed canon packs, a prune citing coverage from
  any *other* canon pack is out of scope for this run — leave the item; the cycle that moves that pack will
  reach it.
- **Never prune a local item that makes a stronger point about a narrower case** than the canon — that isn't
  redundancy. (A local item that only restates the canon in repo-specific names *is* prunable once the canon
  covers the point.)
- **Never let a dedup edit grow an entry or re-import canon prose** — every action removes portable text;
  the skill owns the strip discipline, and the `dedup-prune-integrity` check (this pack) is the backstop
  that reds the session when a dedup-labeled commit grows a local-pack prose file or restates a canon rule.

```
- **Retiring a system by folding its function into another** — audit that the live generator
  moved, not only its past output: a copied directory of old artifacts hides the generator's
  absence, and a stateless recompute over inputs kept for a bounded window starts the series
  shorter than the file it replaced.

  the bare short name returns "no matching tools", which reads exactly like absence. The one
  exception is a server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names: one miss there
  is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query.
- **Polling with an `until` loop** — write a condition that names the state awaited (a file's
  arrival, a run's status): one already true on its first check is a blind sleep wearing a loop,

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. content.content:
1	Below are rules on how to work on this repo.
2	
3	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
4	
5	- **Writing a `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`** — the end state and its rationale only, with
6	  alternatives and their drawbacks. Never requests, prior-state narrative, or owner opinions.
7	
8	
9	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` whose system is now built** — delete it whole rather than trim
10	  it. Verify each section already lives in a module header or pack `README.md` first, and move an
11	  owner-decision record with its rationale. Leave a doc describing work in flight alone. (4)
12	
13	- **Sweeping a deleted design doc's `§`-numbered pointers** — re-point each at a pack README, or
14	  drop it where the sentence only cited itself.
15	
16	- **Having a deferred direction, blocked proposal or status to record** — `docs/`, pointed at from
17	  the issue or PR. Never a pack file: `docs/` is outside the vendor set.
18	
19	- **Ending a session on unfinished work** — write the state into the tracking issue; the owner's
20	  opener is `continue work on #<n>`. Never compose a hand-off prompt.
21	
22	
23	- **Designing anything that spans repos** — split it: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon,
24	  the aggregation half as a Shepherd fleet task. No repo list lives in canon code. (5)
25	
26	- **Landing a derived fleet artifact** — a daily auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file in Shepherd,
27	  never a commit to its `main`.
28	
29	- **Needing a member to flip a platform setting** — last resort; per-repo manual work reliably
30	  does not happen. Prefer the route that works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or neutralise
31	  the blocking behaviour's effect rather than asking for a reconfiguration.
32	
33	- **Requiring a credential nothing weaker can replace** (`FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`) — name the exact
34	  scope, and have the automation report when it is missing rather than degrade silently.
35	
36	- **Landing a change to what members receive** — force delivery only where *"will it work on every
37	  repo?"* is live: engine flow, a contract member files must satisfy, a stub, a migration record, a
38	  new config key. Otherwise the nightly converge is the delivery. (6)
39	
40	- **Forcing fleet delivery** — drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, report per member
41	  unasked, and attach the repos verification needs. A dispatch is not a result; 204 means queued.
42	
43	- **Retiring a field, option or module** — `@deprecated` on its definition, plus a comment at each
44	  sanctioned holdout saying why it still carries the field. Never a bespoke conformance check for a
45	  deprecation; keep the contract validating it.
46	
47	- **Surfacing a number a human reads as a report card** — report a window against the previous
48	  window. Never a monotonic cumulative total, never a figure nothing measures. (9)
49	
50	- **Lacking a field a report-card number needs** — name it absent in the surface's own note. A
51	  stated gap is information, a guess is not. (10)
52	
53	- **Windowing a count** — only where it is built from things that happened inside the window. A
54	  figure derived from a point-in-time stamp reads a steady population as declining. (11)
55	
56	- **Classifying an open object by deriving it from other live state** — reconsider once the
57	  derivation's own inputs can mutate while the object stays open, silently reinterpreting its
58	  history. Prefer a marker stamped once at creation and never revisited.
59	
60	- **Scheduling the removal of a temporary compatibility tolerance** — gate it on a convergence
61	  window the change states for itself, never on a census of members: the canon cannot see which
62	  repos are active, inert or long stale, so "no member still stamps the old format" never reads
63	  true and the tolerance stands forever. (12)
64	
65	## Working with the owner and the session's tools
66	
67	- **Answering "why did it fail?"** — lead with the throwing call site: `file:line`, the function,
68	  and which side enforced it. A narrative that never names the line reads as unanswered.
69	
70	
71	- **Wanting to re-post a question the owner declined** — don't. Take its recommended default, or
72	  open the question up.
73	
74	- **Asking about a vague, destructive-sounding instruction** ("remove the entire mechanism") —
75	  scope the question to the boundary of the vague noun itself, not the consequences of one reading
76	  of it.
77	
78	- **Being asked to generalise something, or to review it** — land the conversions or action points
79	  it unlocks in the same change. A capability ships with its first caller, an analysis with its
80	  first recommendation applied.
81	
82	- **Calling anything on `Claude_Code_Remote`** — one call per intent, ever. Each costs minutes,
83	  and a call that returns nothing has not failed; the retry has run to 81% of a session's tool
84	  wall-clock.
85	
86	
87	- **Needing a session to read issues or PRs across several repos in one pass** — `add_repo`
88	  widens this session's own GitHub scope; unlike file content, issues aren't git refs, so there is
89	  no `git clone` substitute for reaching them.
90	
91	
92	
93	- **Reading a tool result the harness saved to a file** — it is one unbroken line, so `Read`'s
94	  `offset`/`limit` won't shrink it; parse it with `python3 -c 'json.load(...)'` or `jq` instead.
95	
96	- **Re-waiting on a signal that already failed to move** — read the code that governs when it
97	  *can* change before waiting a second time on the same premise.
98	
99	- **Writing a step a human must do by hand into an issue** — make sure it is needed; a checklist
100	  of no-ops teaches the reader to skim it. Link the deepest existing settings URL rather than
101	  writing out a breadcrumb trail. (14)
102	
103	- **Replying to an owner comment that raises more than one claim** — answer every claim in that
104	  first reply, including the one you intend to push back on. (15)
105	
106	- **Repeating a design doc's stated architectural rationale** — verify each claimed ground against
107	  the current code first. "A task structurally cannot hold this permission" is false: code-work
108	  runs inside the executor's own Action job. (16)
109	
110	- **An owner reversing a standing decision** — purge every place in the repo that still states the
111	  old decision (docs, comments, code defaults) and record the new one where a future session reads
112	  it. Answering the prompting question alone is not the fix. (17)
113	
114	
115	- **Running a Bash command with a `cd` outside the project root** — the *next* Bash call silently
116	  resets cwd back to the root ("Shell cwd was reset to …"), whether the first command succeeded or
117	  failed. Prefix every command touching that directory with its own `cd`; a prior one never carries
118	  forward.
119	
120	- **Asserting why a system behaved a certain way** (a park correctly closed, a routing mechanism's
121	  logic) — read the primary evidence, the issue's own body/comments or the enforcing source line,
122	  first. A verdict inferred from structure or memory alone has shipped as a wrongly-merged fix for a
123	  bug that wasn't there.
124	
125	## Checks and capabilities built here
126	
127	- **Starting a new Claudinite-facing capability** — decide which distribution model it is before
128	  writing the first file: a member-local tool, always-on engine code, or an opt-in pack with its
129	  own adoption. Nothing prompts this choice, and getting it wrong costs a move-and-rewrite
130	  cycle. (19)
131	
132	- **Declaring a check, or adding a key to the vocabulary** — name the key so the declaration reads
133	  alone (`scanFiles`, `matchLines`, `relevantWhen`). If it needs a comment to be read, it needs a
134	  better name.
135	
136	- **Adding a legacy tolerance to `engine/` or `packs/`** — file the issue that removes it first,
137	  then put `// @legacy-tolerance advisory:<rule-id|none> retire:#<issue>` on the line directly
138	  above the declaration; `advisory:none` claims no member file can hold the old shape, so that
139	  issue must then name what does read the holder. (68)
140	
141	- **Creating the artifact a check will demand** — create it before the action it gates, not after.
142	
143	- **Changing a per-call hook** (`engine/hooks/*-judge.mjs`, the runner) — you are a guest in the
144	  harness: a judge returns a verdict and `hook-runner.mjs` alone exits, 0 or a deliberate 2;
145	  measure before and after with `node dev/tools/hook-latency.mjs` and record the numbers in the
146	  element's retrospective brief. (70)
147	
148	## The engine, the mount and what reaches members
149	
150	- **Editing `claudinite-scheduler.yml` or `claudinite-executor.yml`** — nothing beyond triggers,
151	  permissions, concurrency and the `run:` line naming an engine module. A converge cannot push to
152	  `.github/workflows/`, so logic left there costs a fleet-wide PR to change.
153	
154	- **Moving a scheduler workflow's program out** — into `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/`, leaving a
155	  single-line `run: node <module>`, and edit both copies — the stub and the canon's own — in the
156	  same commit. `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` blocks the two shapes it can see.
157	
158	- **Writing a path, regex or command against the mount** — the two-root form: the
159	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix optional in a pattern, and a probe for `.claudinite/shared/`
160	  falling back to the repo root. The home runs the same code from the repo root. (26)
161	
162	- **Tightening a contract member-owned files must satisfy** — first ask what carries it across the
163	  fleet. Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only and a migration record moves paths, not
164	  schemas; if nothing carries it, accept the legacy shape in `normalizeManifest`.
165	
166	- **Adding a key to the declared-check spec vocabulary** (`SPEC_KEYS` in `pattern-rules.mjs`) — an
167	  older engine drops that key and runs the rest of the declaration, so the new key buys nothing
168	  until its engine arrives. Write the declaration to be correct without it (#1400).
169	
170	- **A stale member declaration** — fail the run. Never let it degrade to *fewer checks running*.
171	
172	- **Renaming a pack whose config a member writes into their own repo** — a reader of that config
173	  resolves the new key and every legacy spelling, permanently. The rename map fixes code-side ids
174	  only; rewriting the write side reaches just the data the engine owns. (27)
175	
176	
177	- **Extending what a copied stub reads** — make the new config key optional, fail the run when it
178	  is declared-but-unset, and let declaring it trigger a staleness check. Stubs are copied once and
179	  never re-copied, so a new key is dead in every repo holding the old copy. (29)
180	
181	- **Writing a migration record that needs engine behaviour newer than itself** — have `appliesTo`
182	  probe the member's own mount for that capability by content, and stay inert until it reads back;
183	  an unreadable mount reads as "not capable". The executing worker is the member's vendored
184	  one. (30)
185	
186	
187	- **Retiring an emptied `updates/*` export** — read the field: the condition is that no member's
188	  *vendored* worker calls it. Pin the surface with a test carrying an expiry; the canary rehearsal
189	  cannot catch this class.
190	
191	- **Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports** — leave a shim at the old
192	  path re-exporting what it named. The two lanes deliver on separate cycles, so every member spends
193	  a window holding the NEW engine beside an OLD pack. (31)
194	
195	- **Asking which imported symbols are still fielded** — walk the TRUNK's pack history, never
196	  `--all`. An import that only ever existed on an unmerged branch is not fielded. (32)
197	
198	- **Changing a vendored stub** — edit the canon's own `.github/workflows/` copy in the same commit
199	  and diff the two whole files. The canon has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly until it is
200	  a permission denial in production.
201	
202	- **Excluding files from the vendor set by pattern** — whitelist any operational file that matches
203	  by path, and pin it with a test against the real canon tree. The nightly refresh re-runs from
204	  canon HEAD, so a bug there is the one canon regression that is not self-healing. (33)
205	
206	- **Testing that an operational file still vendors** — assert the whole containing directory, not
207	  the one file that broke; otherwise the next file added there needs a fresh edit. (34)
208	
209	- **Retiring or reshaping a protocol the engine exposes** — sweep for callers outside this repo,
210	  not just what greps locally. Two stub copies at the same path declaring different input names is
211	  the same failure from the other side: the two spellings *are* the protocol. (35)
212	
213	- **Branching on the result of an API write in fleet machinery** — read its status, not just the
214	  body. A body-only destructure turns a 403 into a plausible object and the run still logs `ok`.
215	
216	- **Judging whether fleet delivery worked** — members' stamps, never run conclusions. The stamp is
217	  the only artifact that moves.
218	
219	- **A single timeout bound covering two different waits** ("has this started" vs "is something
220	  already running about to finish") — split it, sized from each phase's own declared budget rather
221	  than a round number. (36)
222	
223	- **Writing a give-up message for a hit timeout** — say it is a statement about the clock, not a
224	  verdict on the work. "No successful run yet" sends a reader chasing a settings diagnosis for CI
225	  that was simply still running. (37)
226	
227	- **Writing generated content into a size-capped GitHub API field** — budget it in two tiers: an
228	  always-complete compact summary, plus best-effort detail rationed to a byte budget with an
229	  explicit omitted-count. An unbounded write 422s at the ~64KB cap. (38)
230	
231	- **Writing a generated title whose content scales with a list** — collapse the list to a count
232	  and keep per-item detail in the body. A title is a summary surface, not a second body.
233	
234	- **Preflighting a required grant or permission** — a probe run where the failure's condition
235	  isn't met reports a false-positive pass. Prefer attributing a real observed 403 to the
236	  permission that would fix it. (39)
237	
238	- **Introducing a finer-grained classification of a catch-all state** — default whatever an older
239	  or unaware writer produces to the most conservative member of the new set, so it fails safe
240	  instead of landing in a lane nobody watches.
241	
242	- **Adding a fleet task** — fail loudly on a Context target it cannot reach rather than proceeding
243	  on a partial list, and treat a member as un-adopted until the routine's repo scope names it.
244	  Otherwise the drift completes, filing a report that reads as a full sweep. (40)
245	
246	- **Spawning a child process from a worker** — pass an explicit `cwd`, resolved to a root that
247	  cannot vanish (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`). The converge deletes the tree
248	  its own code-work runs inside.
249	
250	- **A worker crash sharing a benign outcome code** — keep "could not run" distinguishable from
251	  "had nothing to run", or it is unobservable.
252	
253	- **Diagnosing a member's maintenance PR that won't land** — `unstable` beside a green sweep is a
254	  parked `action_required` run, not a missing repo setting.
255	
256	- **Reading a uniform signal across every fleet member** — check for a rate-limit signal before
257	  trusting a uniform empty sweep, and check whether each member's own convergence window has passed
258	  before calling the fleet frozen.
259	
260	- **Corroborating a theory with a signal already known unreliable** — don't. An uncorrected "the
261	  entire fleet is frozen" claim stood for ~10 hours.
262	
263	- **Retiring or migrating a dispatch/config parameter channel** — a parameter that stops being
264	  read must fail loudly, never silently default. A dropped safety knob (`DRY_RUN`) defaults to the
265	  operation's most dangerous mode. (41)
266	
267	- **Relying on a push to trigger further Actions workflows** — a push authored with the default
268	  `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which every converge and auto-merge here uses, fires no `on: push` workflow. Only
269	  a real user or app credential cascades. (42)
270	
271	- **A workflow file referencing a renamed entry point by literal path** — hold a shim open, as for
272	  an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports. `.github/workflows/` lands only through a PR a human
273	  merges. (43)
274	
275	- **A script written for one execution context** — audit every script's environment assumptions (a
276	  real `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `gh`/`curl` reachability) whenever its caller's context changes. Every
277	  script built against the old assumption fails identically, not just the one that broke first.
278	
279	
280	- **Carrying a dotted version identifier** — keep it string-typed everywhere. `'60820.10'` and
281	  `'60820.1'` are different versions and the same float. (46)
282	
283	- **Designing text that instructs a model to echo an exact string** — state the instruction first,
284	  have it disclaim itself as instruction-not-payload, and put the literal string once, last. Never
285	  reference the payload anaphorically ("that line"); recency is what resolves it. (47)
286	
287	## Scheduled tasks
288	
289	- **Filing a verification for a change whose effect first shows in a repo that merely uses
290	  Claudinite** — a run here reads only this repository: its sessions carry no member's scope and
291	  its probes fetch with no credential, so a member's API or private file can never answer.
292	  Reproduce the premise on an object this repo owns, or file the verification on that repo. (71)
293	
294	- **Filing an issue no person will ever act on** — a board, a watermark, the machine's own
295	  bookkeeping — file it CLOSED and labelled, state both on every write so a reopened or
296	  pre-rule one converges, and find it by that label rather than paging the repo's closed
297	  history. (69)
298	
299	- **Opening a queue work-item's own delivered PR** — never `Closes #<the item's own issue>` in
300	  the body. `converge-item.mjs` closes or parks that issue with the right label state; the native
301	  keyword fires on merge regardless and overrides an intended `needs-human-approval` park. (49)
302	
303	- **Choosing a task's cadence** — take it from how often the signal actually moves. A weekly run
304	  still sees all 7 days, because a task's signal window is its own period plus an hour of slack.
305	
306	- **A precondition that fires nearly every night** (one reading `sharedMount`) — daily buys noise,
307	  not freshness, and spends an opus session each time. Prefer weekly where the work isn't
308	  latency-sensitive.
309	
310	- **After any scheduler-mechanism flip** — re-audit every task whose precondition assumed the old
311	  mechanism; grep for `frequency: 'manual'` plus its precondition text, not just the flipped
312	  mechanism's callers. A stale `run: false` becomes a live self-closing landmine. (50)
313	
314	- **Writing a task's precondition** — gate on the objects' own movement in the window (a `touched`
315	  list, a tip-commit date), never on standing state, which is true forever once true. (portable →
316	  `claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md`)
317	
318	- **A precondition signal that is true most days** — let it only *widen* an already-triggered run.
319	
320	- **Scoping a task whose verdict is relative to the rest of a set** — the gate is not the scope:
321	  newness gates, and the full set stays the scope.
322	
323	- **Writing a task whose output is a regenerated file** — land it through
324	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-generated.mjs`, reading prior state from the fetched base, not local
325	  HEAD. (`basics/baselining` is the deliberate exception.)
326	
327	- **A worker that checks out a branch or leaves an index behind** — one executor run drains
328	  several items from one checkout, so it hands the next item a tree it did not expect.
329	
330	- **Wanting to exercise a task Action-side** — dispatch the scheduler workflow with its `wake`
331	  input naming the task; the post-scheduler drain picks it up in the same run. The precondition
332	  still runs at pickup, so a wake that finds no work says so — a verdict, not a failure.
333	
334	- **Converging an unattended run** — do the label/comment/close sequence as the run's very next
335	  action once the outcome is known, never deferred to a checklist recalled at the end of a long
336	  session. (51)
337	
338	- **Closing a run `outcome:done`** — it means nothing is left for anyone to act on. Never while a
339	  PR, branch, or open question from this run is still live.
340	
341	- **Decomposing a pipeline into chained tasks** — chain stages by preconditions that each
342	  re-derive the world's actual state, never by parameters passed forward. A run interrupted
343	  mid-pipeline then self-heals on the next pick.
344	
345	- **Setting `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`** — narrow it to the one stage whose side effect is
346	  genuinely non-idempotent. (52)
347	
348	- **Passing a diagnostic verdict out of a subprocess that may be killed at its timeout ceiling** —
349	  write it to stdout/stderr, never a file written at exit. Already-printed output survives a
350	  `SIGKILL`. (53)
351	
352	- **Writing a repair rule over a live, mutating collection** — a rule gated on *current state*
353	  needs a fresh, targeted read of the item immediately before acting, never the snapshot that
354	  triggered the sweep. A rule gated on a *clock* is safe against snapshot staleness.
355	
356	- **Solving a "must act again later" problem** — check whether an existing generic lane already
357	  carries it before building standing machinery. The deferred-request queue's
358	  `Blocked-by`/`Not-before` lane does.
359	
360	- **Building a dedup or mutex over work items** — key the guard on the target the write lands on,
361	  never the requester's phrasing. A same-title match is blind to two items writing one target under
362	  different titles; `Blocked-by:` is what serializes them. (54)
363	
364	- **Converging a work item from a session** — `converge-item.mjs` prints the calls; making them
365	  verbatim with your own GitHub tools is the whole path, on every session, with or without a REST
366	  route. Hand-fabricating the transition is how an item ends up closed wearing a live status, or
367	  labelled `done` and left open. (2)
368	
369	## Proving a change
370	
371	- **Testing a change to a task's triggering** — drive the real `planSchedulerRun` from a clock at
372	  which the task's anchor has NOT come. Instantiation is decided before any precondition runs, so
373	  starting from a queued item proves only "works once instantiated".
374	
375	- **Testing a fail-soft step** — assert the positive effect (the output IS emitted), never
376	  `status === 0`, which fail-soft makes meaningless. The engine is vendored verbatim, so one
377	  regression disables that step fleet-wide.
378	
379	- **Testing a helper reapplied across a hand-off, a re-queue or a retry** — call it twice and
380	  assert no duplication. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case
381	  corrupts state.
382	
383	- **Testing a mechanism that arbitrates by identity** (a claim, a lock) — the second call must
384	  come from a *different actor*. One actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an
385	  identity-masked race. (55)
386	
387	- **Building a simulator for a stateful engine mechanism** — model what the engine's code actually
388	  *writes*, never the rule's stated *intent*. A sim advancing state wherever the rule's description
389	  matches is correct by construction and blind to where the two diverge.
390	
391	- **Asserting a mid-run invariant** — capture it at the exact moment the state holds. By the end
392	  of the run, normal convergence has cleared the evidence.
393	
394	- **Writing a regression test that pins a policy or convention decision** — assert the
395	  behavior/invariant the decision requires, never a literal sentence quoted from a doc: a
396	  sentence-matching test stays green even while a sibling doc states the opposite, certifying the
397	  contradiction instead of catching it.
398	
399	- **A test that derives its answer by walking git history** — guard explicitly against a shallow
400	  clone and fail loudly. It otherwise passes vacuously exactly when the real answer needs history
401	  it doesn't have. (56)
402	
403	
404	- **Restoring source after a deliberate see-it-fail mutation** — `git checkout -- <file>` at the
405	  moment of mutating, never a `.bak` taken earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in
406	  between. (57)
407	
408	
409	- **Surveying whether something exists in the tree** — a code-search hit is evidence; a miss is
410	  not. Survey by reading each file.
411	
412	- **Documenting or relying on a named knob** — grep for the code that reads it and the code that
413	  writes it first. The corpus naming it is not evidence it exists; all three misses are real
414	  here. (62)
415	
416	- **Deleting a writer** — it is the same change as marking its series historical. Its rows keep
417	  counting plausibly until the retention window ages out, then count nothing. (63)
418	
419	- **Renaming an entity** — sweep for references in code and comments, don't change historical
420	  records, and re-render generated files rather than editing them by hand.
421	
422	- **Sweeping a rename mid-migration across many PRs** — a file added or rewritten after the sweep
423	  starts can independently reinvent the retired constant as a comparison key; a state comparison
424	  against it fails silently, with no error and no failing test, only a wrong count. (3)
425	
426	- **Renaming a word that is also stored data** (a counter key, a wire word, a label) — rename it
427	  on the **decode** side too, or the next encode writes those historical counts as `null`,
428	  silently and only for the old rows.
429	
430	- **A second rename of one name** — map every legacy spelling straight to today's, never chaining
431	  one normalization onto the last, so the oldest vocabulary still normalizes in a single pass. (64)
432	
433	- **Writing a "this period is covered" marker in an idempotent pipeline** — write it strictly
434	  after the durable effect it guards, and scope it to the *declined* case only. A go verdict's
435	  coverage is judged by the item it created, never by the row.
436	
437	- **Verifying a bulk file-move or rewrite sweep preserved content** — check a structural invariant
438	  count before and after (total `test(` calls across the touched files). One sweep truncated 46
439	  test files to zero bytes and every one still "passed".
440	
441	## Editing, branching and merging here
442	
443	
444	
445	- **A JSON target nested inside an array within an entry object** — parse and rewrite
446	  structurally, preserving key order and `via`/`config`/answers by hand. An anchored regex cannot
447	  cross the nested closing bracket, and a fixture without that nesting proves nothing. (65)
448	
449	- **Returning to a branch that waited** — after `git fetch`, re-verify the *premise* unasked: say
450	  whether the problem is still there and what survives. This repo auto-merges its own PRs on top of
451	  migrations that retire whole directories.
452	
453	
454	- **Merging a PR that has sat open across many `main` commits** — check its current
455	  `mergeable_state`, not an old green CI run. A structural change on `main` since (a directory
456	  move, a renamed path) can turn a once-clean branch conflicted without a new run ever failing.
457	
458	- **After a PR lands by squash-merge** — `git remote prune origin` before touching that branch
459	  again. GitHub deletes the head ref here, so a stale tracking ref makes the next push reject and
460	  the stop hook report phantom local work. (67)
461	
462	
463	
464	- **Merging in a session that also has a consumer repo in its sources** — resolve the merge skill
465	  by *target repo*, not by which matched first. The consumer's wins on name, silently skipping the
466	  canon-only post-merge conversation capture
467	  (`node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), which is part of the merge.
468	
469	- **Having work that completes or corrects an open PR** — put it on that PR's branch. A dispatch
470	  prompt's designated branch routes work, not review; splitting gives the owner two gates for one
471	  decision.
472	
473	- **Wanting to combine two PRs** — update the one you're keeping and close the other. Never push
474	  one's branch onto the other's base: GitHub marks a PR merged once its head is reachable, and a
475	  later `state: closed` is a no-op. Check the API's `merged` field before reporting.
476	
477	- **Being asked "should no X decide this?"** — it questions whether the decision exists at all;
478	  never answer by relocating the knob one rung out. Ask who would set it differently and why that
479	  can't be read off the structure.
480	
481	- **Facing a retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe** — check whether declining to
482	  retry removes the uncertainty before building dedup machinery to manage it.
483	
484	- **Writing a regex import-path rewriter for a bulk file-move** — anchor to real import/export
485	  syntax (line-start, or after a specific separator), never a bare `from '...'` searched across the
486	  whole text. A fixture embedding import syntax as string data matches identically and is corrupted.
487	
488	- **Running the prose-to-checks sweep here** — the worklist is
489	  `docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md`, every rule classified by the moment that could
490	  carry it; convert from its A–F rows, and correct a mis-read row there, dated, rather than
491	  re-deriving the class.
